name: Cynic self-sufficiency through rejection of convention
plain_explanation: The Cynics held that true virtue and freedom come from wanting as little as possible from the world, so that nothing external -- poverty, insult, loss -- can touch you. Diogenes lived this out literally, owning almost nothing and living by begging.
precise_definition: The doctrine that virtue and moral freedom consist in liberation from desire for external, fortune-dependent goods (wealth, honour, comfort, convention), achieved by deliberately rejecting the artificial trappings of civilization ('defacing the coinage' of all conventional values).
why_it_mattered: Russell treats it as the doctrine's most valuable core, later inherited wholesale by the Stoics, though the Stoics -- unlike the Cynics -- did not reject the amenities of civilization itself.
historical_origin: Develops from Antisthenes (a disciple of Socrates) through his pupil Diogenes of Sinope in the fourth century B.C., though its temper, Russell notes, belongs to the Hellenistic age despite predating it slightly.
examples: Diogenes living by begging and owning almost nothing
His reply to Alexander's offer of any favor: 'only to stand out of my light'
Diogenes's view that Prometheus was justly punished for giving mankind the arts of civilization
objections: Popularized Cynicism (Teles) degenerated into using 'indifference to goods' as an excuse to accept charity without gratitude or obligation
competing_positions: Stoicism, which retained the ideal of indifference to fortune but did not reject civilized life itself
The Taoists, Rousseau, and Tolstoy, whom Russell compares to Diogenes but judges less consistent
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly absorbed into Stoic ethics (Ch. XXVIII): indifference to external fortune as the basis of virtue and freedom.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rejects government, private property, marriage, and established religion outright.
